facts.statement: Elornis is an extinct genus of flamingo that lived in the Late Oligocene of Ronzon, France.
facts.quote: Elornis is an extinct genus of flamingo from the Late Oligocene of Ronzon, France.

facts.statement: The name Elornis was coined in the 1850s but remained invalid until Henri Milne-Edwards published descriptions later.
facts.quote: Although the name was coined in the 1850s, the name remained a nomen nudum until later publications by French zoologist Henri Milne-Edwards.

facts.statement: Auguste Aymard first coined the name Elornis in 1855 during a report presented to the Congres Seientifique de France.
facts.quote: The name Elornis was first coined by Auguste Aymard in a report on the paleontology of the French Haute Loire region, which was presented on two occasions to the Congres Seientifique de France in 1855.

facts.statement: Aymard's original report only stated that the birds were flamingos without providing a full description or illustrations.
facts.quote: However, very little information is given in the report, only stating that these birds are flamingos and neither giving a full description nor illustrating the material.

facts.statement: Henri Milne-Edwards is credited as the authority for Elornis because Aymard's original names were considered nomina nuda.
facts.quote: Thus, instead of Aymard being credited as the authority behind Elornis, it would have to be Milne-Edwards.

facts.statement: Aymard's original fossil material was presumed lost, leaving only Milne-Edwards' descriptions and illustrations as available data.
facts.quote: Aymard's original material was presumed lost, with the descriptions and illustrations given by Milne-Edwards being the only available data.

facts.statement: Elornis littoralis was described by Milne-Edwards based on postcranial remains such as the pelvis, tarsometatarsi, tibiotarsi, and furculae.
facts.quote: Elornis littoralis, as described by Milne-Edwards, was based on various postcranial remains including the pelvis, tarsometatarsi, tibiotarsi and furculae.

facts.statement: Lydekker named a fourth species, Elornis (?) anglicus, in 1891.
facts.quote: One more species was named by Lydekker in 1891, designated Elornis (?) anglicus.

facts.statement: Later research moved Lydekker's Elornis (?) anglicus to the genus Actiornis and identified it as an ibis.
facts.quote: Later research however placed this species in the genus Actiornis and recovered it as an ibis.

facts.statement: Elornis has historically been classified as a member of the Phoenicopteridae, though recent research suggests it may be more basal.
facts.quote: Elornis has been historically considered to be a member of the Phoenicopteridae, but more recent research suggests it may have been more basal.

facts.statement: Elornis lived during the Rupelian stage, from 33.9 to 27.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Rupelian (33.9 to 27.3 million years ago)

facts.statement: Research on Elornis is difficult because the current location of the fossil material is unknown, limiting data to Milne-Edwards' descriptions and illustrations.
facts.quote: Research on this taxon is however difficult as the current whereabouts of the fossil material are unknown, limiting data to the description and illustrations of Milne-Edwards.

rejected.statement: Elornis grandis received little attention, with its intended holotype humerus only described as being 'as big as that of a flamingo' and not illustrated.
rejected.quote: Elornis grandis received less attention, the humerus Aymard intended as the holotype only mentioned to be 'as big as that of a flamingo' by Milne-Edwards and not illustrated at all.
